Dear Senator Nicole Grohoski, Representative Kristen Cloutier, and members of the Taxation Committee,
My name is Ann Dodd-Collins. I live in Portland, and I am writing in support of LD 1294, "An Act to Expand the Dependent Exemption Tax Credit".
In 2023, 12.6% of Maine kids lived in poverty. The Dependent Exemption Tax Credit (DETC) helps families with kids or dependent adults pay for what they need. LD 1294 would double the current tax credit. It would provide an additional $300 for dependents under age 6, and it would be more targeted to families with low and middle income. Importantly, the proposal is revenue neutral because it pays for itself by phasing out the benefit for Maine's highest earners who need the support less.
Many families in Maine struggle to afford basic needs like food, rent, fuel, and child care. Although my youngest child is 41 years old, I remember the struggle to meet my family's needs. I became an expert at "robbing Peter to pay Paul". I paid my mortgage late one month, another month the payment to CMP was late. And almost every month I had to use my credit card to cover some unexpected expense. But we survived. It's much harder for families today. Wages have not kept up with inflation and the price of basic necessities has skyrocketed.
Helping families in Maine who are struggling to afford basic needs like food, rent, fuel, and child care creates a better future for everyone. I urge you to vote Ought To Pass on LD 1294.

For all these reasons, LD 1294 is the right thing to do. It's the moral thing to do. And we at the Maine Council of Churches urge you to vote "ought to pass" on LD 1294.

Joint Standing Committee on Taxation Tuesday, April 8, 2025
Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation, I am writing on behalf of the Maine Coalition to End Domestic Violence (MCEDV) in support of LD 1294.
Most survivors of domestic abuse and violence in Maine experience economic abuse from their partner. Financial issues create real and lasting barriers to survivors separating from the person causing them harm, and child support is rarely paid as ordered by the court. In response to what we have learned from survivors about the prevalence of economic abuse and the barriers to safety and stability it presents, MCEDV and our member programs have built our capacity both to talk to survivors about their financial struggles and to help support survivors in addressing these issues. Through this work with survivors, we have seen that a little goes a long way.
Through private philanthropy, MCEDV has been able to create and sustain our Liberation Fund, which allows advocates across the state to help survivors with concrete financial needs that a survivor articulates as a barrier to safety. This has included things like: paying for new tires for their car, so that they can get to work and get their children to school; covering the cost of next semester's textbooks as they continue their education; paying an overdue credit card bill, so that it doesn't go into collections and damage their credit; and supporting the cost of getting utilities turned back on. What we have observed through our Liberation Fund program is that just the relatively small amount of financial support that we are able to offer (the average request of our fund is less than $600 per survivor) can be enough to support a family with no to low income to live and work in their community more safely and with greater stability. Doubling the state Dependent Exemption Tax Credit will make a difference to the families who receive it in much the same way. An extra $300 may not seem like much, but when you need groceries, gas and car repairs, school supplies, and yet another pair of new shoes, it feels huge. We see this every time we successfully expand credits that benefit families with low and moderate incomes. Putting just a little more money in a family's hands to spend on the things they need most can be transformational.

For so many of the survivors that our network supports, just a little bit of help decreases economic barriers to creating a safe and stable independent household for themselves and their child, away from the person harming them. This is one way to increase the long-term wellbeing of children in Maine, a wise investment at any point in time. We urge you to support LD 1294 to help parents, including those who have survived domestic abuse, to create safe and stable homes. Thank you.

Sen. Grohoski, Rep. Cloutier, and honorable members of the Taxation Committee, my name is Lori Baugh-Castellano, I live in Lisbon, and I submit this testimony in support of LD 1294, expanding Maine's Dependent Exemption Tax Credit for children under six in families with low and moderate incomes.
Expanding Maine's dependent exemption tax credit is important for us because it will be a direct investment in the lives of kids who could really use that investment. Stability is important for children-I know this from firsthand experience.
My wife and I became foster parents because we cared about kids. There's such a huge need for foster parents; it's amazing how many emails we get every week highlighting kids who need care. We are currently making a home for seven kids, ranging from 5 months to 18 years, and we maintain a supportive relationship with another child we previously fostered.
Two years ago, we brought home a newborn from the hospital. We have been present for his first smiles and his first steps, and we've cared for him through everything from colds to kidney surgery. We will finalize his adoption later this month. Meanwhile, we've welcomed another baby into the family. I'm sixty years old and I like my sleep, but I give it up to care for these children.
We love our kids and do our best for them, but thereisa financial cost, and the stipends we receive as foster parents don't begin to cover everything. Diapers and formula are expensive, and the little ones grow out of their clothes long before they wear them out. Food costs for the older kids keep rising. It's harder to do things with the older kids when the younger ones are so care-intensive, but they all pitch in and help. I've been thinking that a double stroller might make whole-family outings easier; this is the kind of expense that this tax credit could help with.
When we first became foster parents, my wife and I were both working full time and trying to do it all. I had a good job, but combining that with caring for and chauffeuring so many kids with various needs was exhausting. Now I'm the stay-at-home parent and I'm putting the kids first. When we adopt our two-year-old, his preschool will no longer be covered by the state and he'll have to come home. Care has a cost, and someone has to bear it.
We are doing the best we can to help these kids have bright futures. I urge you to do the same. Invest in Maine's children by passing LD 1294.

Testimonial for LD1294 (Maine CTC/DETC)
Thank you, Senator Grohowski, Representative Cloutier and distinguished members of the Taxation Committee. My name is Meghann Carrasco, and I am writing in support of LD 1294, "An Act to Expand the Dependent Exemption Tax Credit." This proposed bill represents a critical opportunity to directly support working families in Maine.
LD 1294 proposes a $300 tax credit for families earning less than $150,000 per year for each dependent child under the age of six. This bill is targeting specific support for low and middle income families without costing the state additional money.
I am a founder of a nonprofit childcare center in Gorham, Maine and a mother of two boys. I work with families of all socioeconomic backgrounds and we specifically work hard to support our families to help access important programs to buffer the cost of living while raising families. I know this tax credit would be crucial in helping many people make ends meet and support their bottom lines.
As a parent and working Mainer, I have felt the effects of the cost of living increases. This tax credit would have a great impact working families across Maine. In 2023, 12.6% of Maine's children lived in poverty, and many families are struggling to afford food, rent, fuel, and childcare. This is where the Dependent Exemption Tax Credit comes in--it's money that parents and caregivers can use for whatever their family needs most, whether that's paying for doctor visits, car repairs, rent, or even just keeping the lights on.
Investing in Maine's child tax credit isn't just a win for families today--it's a smart long-term investment in our future. Studies show that for every $1 spent on the federal child tax credit (of which the DETC is Maine's version), $10 is returned to the economy. Helping families now will contribute to a stronger, more stable future for everyone in Maine.
This would not be a "hand out", but an investment in our state's working families. Please vote "ought to pass" on LD 1294 and show your constituents that you recognize the struggles we are facing and that you care enough to act.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Meghann Carrasco Westbrook, ME

For tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, the bill proposes to double the dependent exemption tax credit to $600 for each qualifying dependent
who has not attained 6 years of age before the close of the taxable year. The bill
also proposes to accelerate the phase-out of the credit by reducing the credit by $20 for each $500 by which the taxpayer's Maine adjusted gross income exceeds $100,000 if filing single or married separate, $125,000 if filing head of household, and $150,000 if filing married joint or as a surviving spouse.
Currently, the dependent exemption tax credit is equal to $300 for each
qualifying child and dependent of the taxpayer for whom the federal child tax
credit was claimed for the same taxable year. The credit is subject to a phaseout equal to $7.50 for each $1,000 by which the taxpayer's Maine adjusted gross income exceeds $400,000 for married taxpayers filing jointly and $200,000 for all other taxpayers. The credit for part-year residents and nonresidents is prorated based on the ratio of income taxable to Maine.

inflation.
The Maine dependent exemption tax credit was created to replace the personal exemption for dependents after the federal Tax Cuts and Jobs Act suspended the federal personal exemption deduction for tax years 2018 through 2025 and increased the federal child tax credit. It is unclear Whether the federal
changes will be allowed to revert, be extended, or be modified in some way. Due
to this uncertainty, the Department recommends that the changes proposed by this bill be delayed until tax years beginning January l, 2026 - thereby giving the State the time and ability to react to any federal changes to the federal credits and exemptions on which the state credit is based.
This bill adds another phase-out of a tax benefit that will increase the effective marginal tax rate on upper-middle income households by 4 percentage
